implementation_notes: functools.reduce is the standard library's fold: it applies its two-argument function cumulatively, left to right - reduce(lambda x, y: x + y, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) computes ((((1+2)+3)+4)+5) - and takes an optional initial value that is placed before the elements. It is the general form (any carrier, any binary combine) and the right tool when no builtin expresses the algebra; where a builtin does exist, Python's own style is to prefer it (sum, any, all, min, max, math.prod, str.join, or a plain for loop), because those are C-implemented, state the operation in the call and short-circuit where possible. There is no right fold in the stdlib: a right-associative combine means reversed() plus reduce, or a recursive function.
code_sketch:
from functools import reduce

total = reduce(lambda acc, o: acc + o.amount, orders, 0)      # explicit algebra + identity

# right-associative combine: reverse first (reversed() is lazy, reduce is not)
expr = reduce(lambda rest, x: f"({x} {rest})", reversed(items), "end")
pitfalls: reduce is left-associative by construction and there is no reduceRight: pasting a right-nesting combine into it silently produces the wrong association rather than an error.

The accumulator is rebound (not mutated) at each step: returning a container that the step also mutated in place, or starting from a shared mutable initial, leads to aliasing surprises that no type checker reports.

Omitting the initial value makes reduce raise TypeError on an empty iterable and seed from the first element otherwise, so the identity element has to be chosen deliberately instead of omitted by accident.

variants.name: Builtin aggregates as the fold for monoids
variants.idiom_name: sum, any, all, min, max, math.prod, str.join
variants.implementation_notes: When the combine is a monoid the language has already absorbed the fold: sum(iterable, start) is the + monoid (with math.fsum documented as the accuracy-preserving alternative for floats and ''.join as the string spelling), math.prod(iterable, start=1) is the * monoid since 3.8, any/all are the boolean monoids and short-circuit - which makes them the fold that stops - min/max are the idempotent choice operators, and str.join is the string monoid. These are C-implemented, faster than an equivalent reduce, and they name the algebra in the call; the price is that they cover only their own monoid, so a custom combine still falls back to reduce or an explicit loop.
variants.code_sketch:
total   = sum(o.amount for o in orders)          # + monoid, C speed
product = math.prod(prices, start=1)             # * monoid (Python 3.8+)
ok      = all(v > 0 for v in values)             # short-circuiting boolean monoid
joined  = ", ".join(names)                       # the string monoid
pitfalls: sum over floats accumulates in iteration order without compensation: math.fsum is the documented replacement for accuracy, and sum deliberately refuses strings (use ''.join) to keep quadratic concatenation visible.

any/all short-circuit, so a predicate with side effects runs only until the result is decided - the effect count depends on the data, which is a feature for validation and a trap for profiling or logging.
These builtins consume a generator: a generator argument is exhausted by the aggregate, so a second pass over the same object yields nothing while the same fold over a list can be re-run.

variants.name: Hand-written structural fold over dataclasses with match
variants.idiom_name: match statement over class patterns of dataclass cases
variants.implementation_notes: For a recursive data type Python's idiom is a recursive function that pattern-matches the node: frozen dataclasses (or NamedTuple) for the cases, a match statement with class patterns for the dispatch (PEP 634, Python 3.10) and one call per child position. The match statement removes the isinstance cascade and makes the cases readable, but Python performs no exhaustiveness analysis, so the last arm must be a catch-all that raises - it is load-bearing, and a case added without extending the match becomes a runtime error at best and a silently wrong branch at worst. This is the only realization of the pattern for genuine tree folds in Python; functools.reduce and the builtin aggregates cover linear structures only.
variants.code_sketch:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Lit: v: int
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Add: l: "Expr"; r: "Expr"
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Mul: l: "Expr"; r: "Expr"
Expr = Lit | Add | Mul

def evaluate(e: Expr) -> int:
    match e:
        case Lit(v):    return v
        case Add(l, r): return evaluate(l) + evaluate(r)
        case Mul(l, r): return evaluate(l) * evaluate(r)
        case _:         raise TypeError(f"unhandled case: {e!r}")
pitfalls: match has no exhaustiveness check and no compiler assistance: the wildcard arm is the only thing standing between a new case and a silently wrong result, so the match must raise rather than return a default.

CPython's recursion limit (sys.getrecursionlimit(), 1000 by default) is reached long before memory is, and every fold level costs at least one frame (usually several with match): input-driven depth needs an explicit stack or an increased limit with a matching stack budget.

dataclass(frozen=True) cases make the algebra pure and hashable but allocate a new object per rebuilt case, so an accumulating fold over a large tree should fold into a mutable carrier (dict/list) instead of rebuilding cases.
